What is CNC Technology? CNC technology refers to the integrated use of software, control systems, and automated machinery to manage and execute precision manufacturing processes. In modern production environments, CNC technology functions as a core manufacturing platform—linking digital design data with machining operations, tool management, and quality control systems. Advantages of CNC Technology CNC technology offers a wide range of advantages that make it essential to modern manufacturing. By combining computer-controlled automation with high-performance machinery, CNC systems significantly improve manufacturing efficiency. They also enable superior quality and scalability across diverse industries. High Precision and Consistent Accuracy One of the most significant advantages of CNC technology is its ability to deliver extremely high precision. CNC technology can repeatedly produce components with tight tolerances that are difficult or impossible to achieve through manual machining. Once a program is validated, the same dimensions and surface quality can be maintained across thousands of parts, ensuring consistent accuracy even in complex geometries. This level of precision is especially critical in industries such as aerospace, automotive, medical devices, and electronics, where small dimensional deviations can affect performance, safety, or compliance with industry standards. Increased Production Efficiency CNC technology dramatically improves production efficiency by automating machining operations. Machines can run continuously with minimal operator intervention, reducing setup time and accelerating production cycles. Multi-axis CNC systems further enhance efficiency by completing multiple operations—such as milling, drilling, and contouring—in a single setup. Automated tool changes, optimized tool paths, and high-speed machining capabilities allow manufacturers to shorten lead times and respond quickly to changing production demands. Excellent Repeatability and Quality Control Repeatability is a core strength of CNC technology. Every part produced from the same CNC program is virtually identical, minimizing variation and reducing scrap rates. This repeatability simplifies quality control processes, as fewer manual inspections are required once a process is stabilized. CNC systems also integrate easily with in-process measurement and inspection technologies, enabling real-time quality monitoring and early detection of deviations before defects occur. Material and Design Versatility CNC technology supports a wide range of materials, including metals, plastics, composites, and engineered alloys. From aluminum and stainless steel to advanced polymers and titanium, CNC machines can be optimized to handle different cutting characteristics and surface finish requirements. A common example is aluminum CNC machining , which is widely used due to aluminum’s excellent machinability and strength-to-weight ratio. In addition, CNC technology enables the machining of complex shapes, internal features, and intricate contours that would be extremely time-consuming or impractical with conventional methods. This design freedom allows engineers to innovate without being limited by manufacturing constraints. Scalability from Prototyping to Mass Production Another key advantage of CNC technology is its scalability. The same CNC setup can be used for rapid prototyping, small-batch production, and high-volume manufacturing with minimal modification. Design changes can be implemented quickly by updating the digital program rather than retooling entire production lines. This flexibility is particularly valuable for startups, R&D teams, and manufacturers operating in fast-moving markets where product iterations are frequent. Reduced Labor Dependency and Improved Safety By automating machining tasks, CNC technology reduces reliance on manual labor and lowers the risk of human error. Operators are less exposed to cutting tools and moving machine components, resulting in a safer working environment. Modern CNC systems also feature built-in safety controls, error detection, and machine monitoring functions that further protect both personnel and equipment while maintaining stable production. Cost Efficiency Over the Product Lifecycle While CNC machines require an initial investment, they offer long-term cost advantages. Reduced material waste, lower rework rates, shorter production times, and improved machine utilization all contribute to a lower cost per part over the product lifecycle. For manufacturers seeking consistent quality, predictable output, and efficient resource usage, CNC technology represents a cost-effective solution that supports sustainable growth. Applications of CNC Technology in Manufacturing CNC technology has a wide range of applications across industries due to its ability to deliver high precision, consistency, and production efficiency. From large-scale industrial manufacturing to rapid prototyping, CNC technology continues to expand as materials, software, and machine capabilities evolve. Applications in Metalworking CNC milling machines, lathes, and laser cutters handle metals like aluminum, steel, and titanium with unmatched precision. These machines reduce manual labor, minimize errors, and allow for complex shapes that meet rigorous industry standards. In metalworking industries where tolerance control and material consistency are critical, CNC technology enables reliable production of complex metal components at scale. Applications in Plastics and Woodworking Beyond metals, CNC routers can cut, engrave, and shape plastic components or wood panels with high accuracy. Routers are typically used for wood and plastic materials, while milling machines are better suited for metal machining due to their rigidity and cutting capabilities. Manufacturers can efficiently produce prototypes and mass-produced items, lowering production costs and turnaround times. Industrial Applications Industries such as automotive, aerospace, electronics, energy, and heavy machinery rely on CNC systems to produce structural components, housings, brackets, and precision parts. CNC machining ensures tight tolerances, repeatability, and high reliability for critical components. Prototyping and Small Batch Production Rapid prototyping and small-batch CNC production allow engineers to quickly transform digital designs into functional prototypes, enabling faster design validation, iterative testing, and reduced time-to-market. Innovative Uses in Various Industries Advanced applications such as multi-axis cutting, hybrid additive-subtractive manufacturing, and complex 3D contour machining expand possibilities in medical devices, architecture, and custom design. CNC Machine Technology Types of CNC Machines CNC machine technology includes milling machines, lathes, routers, plasma cutters, and laser engraving systems. Each type serves a specific function, from cutting and drilling to shaping and engraving, meeting diverse manufacturing needs. How CNC Machines Work CNC machines operate by translating digital designs into precise machining actions through integrated control systems. This enables highly accurate and repeatable production while minimizing material waste and optimizing workflow efficiency. Maintenance and Optimization Proper maintenance of CNC machines is essential for long-term performance. Regular calibration, tool replacement, and software updates optimize machine efficiency and prevent downtime. Skilled operators can further enhance productivity by choosing the right tooling and machining parameters. Industrial CNC Technology Automation in Large-Scale Production Industrial CNC technology enables full automation of production lines. Large-scale manufacturing can run continuously with minimal human supervision, improving throughput and reducing labor costs. Integration with Industrial Processes CNC technology integrates seamlessly with industrial processes such as assembly, quality inspection, and material handling. This integration allows for smarter factories, streamlined workflows, and higher overall efficiency. Case Studies Industries adopting industrial CNC technology have reported reduced production errors, faster turnaround times, and improved product consistency. For example, automotive suppliers use CNC machines to produce engine components with precise tolerances, enhancing vehicle performance and reliability. CNC Technology Services Design and Consulting Services CNC technology services extend beyond machining itself. Design and consulting services help manufacturers apply CNC technology effectively by optimizing material selection, machining strategies, and process planning before production begins. Manufacturing and Prototyping Services Service providers offer CNC machining for both prototypes and mass production. This allows businesses to outsource specialized tasks, reduce overhead, and maintain high-quality standards. Maintenance and Support Services Many CNC technology service providers also offer ongoing maintenance, troubleshooting, and training. This ensures clients can maintain efficient operations, extend machine lifespan, and minimize production delays. Future Trends in CNC Technology Beyond basic CNC operation and machine control, future CNC technology development is increasingly driven by intelligence, connectivity, and system-level integration. Future developments will not only improve precision and productivity but also fundamentally reshape how factories operate, how products are designed, and how manufacturers compete in global markets. Smart CNC and AI Integration The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with CNC systems is transforming machining from reactive automation into predictive and adaptive manufacturing. AI-powered algorithms can analyze historical machining data. They automatically optimize tool paths, reduce cycle times, and minimize tool wear. Machine learning models are increasingly used to detect subtle signs of tool degradation or misalignment before they cause defects. In aerospace and medical device manufacturing, where tolerances are extremely tight, AI-assisted CNC tool path optimization is already being adopted to ensure consistency and precision across complex geometries. Over time, smart CNC machines will be able to adjust cutting strategies in real time, self-correcting for material inconsistencies and dynamic load variations without human intervention. Sensors embedded in CNC equipment collect real-time data on temperature, vibration, spindle load, and tool life. This data, streamed through secure networks, feeds into centralized manufacturing execution systems (MES) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems to support real-time monitoring and informed decision-making. Connected CNC machines can automatically schedule maintenance based on actual usage patterns, reducing unplanned downtime. In facilities with multiple machines producing different parts, IoT connectivity enhances workflow coordination, material tracking, and quality control, leading to higher operational efficiency and lower production costs. Advanced Materials and Machining Techniques As new materials continue to emerge, CNC technology evolves to address the challenges they present. Advanced composites, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) , and next-generation polymers have unique machining requirements. High-entropy alloys are composed of multiple principal elements in near-equal proportions, offering exceptional strength, wear resistance, and thermal stability. These materials are increasingly used in aerospace and energy applications, where CNC machining must precisely control cutting forces and heat generation to maintain part integrity. CNC technology is also incorporating hybrid manufacturing techniques that combine additive manufacturing (3D printing) with traditional subtractive machining. These hybrid processes allow complex internal structures to be built additively and then finished with high-precision CNC cutting, making them ideal for lightweight aerospace components and customized medical implants. Human–Machine Collaboration and Augmented Reality Future CNC environments will emphasize human–machine collaboration, where operators work alongside intelligent machining systems rather than simply monitoring them. Augmented reality (AR) tools will support setup, training, and maintenance by overlaying digital instructions directly onto physical machinery. Technicians wearing AR headsets will be guided step-by-step through complex calibration or repair processes, reducing training time and lowering the risk of error. Furthermore, virtual simulation environments will allow engineers to preview machining operations before any material is cut. This not only helps validate designs but also ensures that tooling and fixturing are optimized for efficiency and safety. Conclusion Summary of Key Benefits CNC technology has transformed modern manufacturing by improving precision, efficiency, and flexibility. It enables complex machining, reduces errors, and accelerates production cycles. Impact on Modern Manufacturing With industrial CNC technology, advanced machines, and comprehensive services, manufacturers can achieve high-quality output, innovate rapidly, and maintain a competitive edge. As CNC technology continues to evolve, its influence on the manufacturing industry will only grow stronger. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - M5StackChan AI Desktop Robot PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - M5StackChan AI Desktop Robot by: PCBWay Sep 24,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCBWay Store Link： AI Desktop Robot StackChan is a super kawaii AI desktop robot co-created by M5Stack and the user community. It uses the M5Stack flagship IoT development kit CoreS3 as its main controller, powered by an ESP32-S3 SoC featuring a 240 MHz dual-core processor, with 16MB Flash and 8MB PSRAM onboard, and supporting Wi-Fi and BLE. The main unit also integrates a 2.0-inch capacitive touch display with a high-strength glass cover, a 0.3 MP camera, a proximity & ambient light sensor, a 9-axis IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope + magnetometer), a microSD card slot, a 1W speaker, dual microphones, and power/reset buttons. The robot body, connected to the main unit, includes a USB-C interface for power and data, a 550 mAh battery, two feedback servos (360-degree continuous rotation on the horizontal axis and 90-degree movement on the vertical axis), two rows totaling 12 RGB LEDs, infrared transmitter and receiver, a three-zone touch panel, and a full-featured NFC module. The factory firmware is feature-rich, including an AI Agent, lively and expressive animations, ESP-NOW wireless remote control, and online app downloads. It can connect to a mobile app for video viewing, remote avatar control, and more, and also supports online updates (OTA). The product also supports programming via Arduino, UiFlow2, and other methods, and can connect to various expansion units in the M5Stack ecosystem, making it easy to implement a wide range of custom functions. Verify Now Blog > 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling by: Mila Sep 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor 0402 capacitor 0603 capacitor 0402 vs 0603 capacitor A common misconception is that a larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better filtering performance. However, in high-speed PCB designs such as FPGA, SoC, and DDR applications, 0402 capacitors with a typical value of 0.1 μF are commonly placed near BGA core power pins instead of larger 0603 capacitors. For the same nominal capacitance, the key difference in 0402 vs 0603 capacitor performance is not how much charge the capacitor stores, but its equivalent series inductance (ESL). At lower frequencies, the performance difference between package sizes is usually less significant. As the operating frequency enters the MHz range and above, ESL increasingly affects the impedance and effective frequency range of a decoupling capacitor. The Underlying Principle: Equivalent Series Inductance (ESL) A surface-mount capacitor is not an ideal capacitor. Its equivalent circuit typically consists of an ideal capacitance (C), equivalent series resistance (ESR), and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL comes from the entire current path, including the internal electrodes, terminations, PCB pads, traces, and power/ground vias. Inductance opposes rapidly changing current, and its effect becomes more significant as frequency increases. Every capacitor has a self-resonant frequency (SRF): Operating frequency < SRF: The device behaves mainly as a capacitor and can perform its decoupling function normally. Operating frequency > SRF: The device gradually becomes inductive, and its high-frequency decoupling capability decreases. A higher self-resonant frequency generally means that a decoupling capacitor can maintain low impedance over a wider high-frequency range. For example, consider 0402 and 0603 capacitors with the same nominal capacitance of 0.1 μF: 0603 capacitor: Its larger body size generally results in a longer internal current path and higher intrinsic parasitic inductance. 0402 capacitor: Its smaller body size generally provides a shorter current path and lower intrinsic parasitic inductance. When an IC core suddenly draws high-frequency transient current, the total inductance of the current loop affects the power response. Even a capacitor with excellent electrical characteristics may provide limited high-frequency decoupling if the current path is too long. Therefore, the choice between an 0402 vs 0603 capacitor should not be based on a fixed frequency boundary. As frequency increases, the ESL differences introduced by the component package and PCB mounting structure become increasingly important. The actual selection should consider effective capacitance, ESR, ESL, SRF, and the PCB layout together. Package size is only one factor affecting parasitic inductance. The total power-to-ground loop inductance is more important. As the package becomes smaller, the reduction in ESL can provide diminishing returns because the PCB mounting structure can become a larger part of the total inductance. At the same time, soldering difficulty, placement requirements, and component costs may increase. During decoupling capacitor selection and PDN impedance simulation, models that match the actual component and PCB mounting structure should be used whenever possible. Otherwise, the simulated impedance curve and resonance characteristics may differ significantly from the actual result. For high-speed PCB decoupling, component selection should therefore go beyond nominal capacitance. The package, effective capacitance, ESL, SRF, and—most importantly—the complete current-loop PCB layout should all be considered. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Can AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly in ADC PCB Design? by: Mila Sep 24,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout agnd vs dgnd mixed-signal PCB design ADC PCB layout When designing an ADC or DAC, one of the most common questions in PCB layout is how to handle the AGND and DGND pins. If a device has separate analog and digital ground pins, should they be connected directly, separated into different ground planes, or joined at a single point? This question is especially important in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design, where fast digital switching currents can potentially interfere with sensitive analog circuits. To understand the right approach to AGND vs DGND, the key is not simply whether the two grounds are connected, but how the return currents flow through the PCB. (schematic with AGND & GND) Why Do ADCs and DACs Have Separate AGND and DGND Pins? An ADC can be roughly understood as having two different domains. One side contains the sampling circuit, op amp, reference, comparator, PGA, DAC core, and analog bias circuits. These belong to the analog domain. The other side contains the SPI/I²C interface, digital logic, registers, clock, state machine, and other digital circuits. These belong to the digital domain. One of the biggest characteristics of digital circuits is that their current can change very quickly. For example, when an SPI interface operates at tens of MHz, every clock transition can generate transient current. These currents need to form a complete return path through the power and ground network. This is where the problem begins. Assume the digital return current is: ID = 50 mA and it flows through a PCB trace with only: R = 20 mΩ The resulting ground voltage variation is: V = IR = 50 mA × 20 mΩ = 1 mV. 1 mV may look very small, but it is not necessarily negligible for a high-resolution ADC. For example, consider a 16-bit ADC with a 2.5 V full-scale range: 1 LSB ≈ 2.5 V / 65536 ≈ 38.1 μV Therefore, a 1 mV ground voltage variation corresponds to approximately: 1 mV / 38.1 μV ≈ 26 LSB Of course, the actual ADC conversion error depends on how this ground disturbance couples into the analog input, reference, and internal circuits. However, this example illustrates an important point: For a high-precision ADC, the key concern is not simply how low the ground resistance is, but where the digital return current flows. This is one of the fundamental considerations in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly? In many designs, AGND and DGND ultimately connect to the same ground reference. However, there is an important condition: this does not mean that AGND and DGND can simply be connected with two arbitrary traces and left at that. If the ADC or DAC datasheet specifies that AGND and DGND should be connected close to the device, follow the manufacturer's recommended layout. For many high-precision ADCs and DACs, the recommended PCB layout is designed to maintain a low-impedance, low-inductance connection between AGND and DGND while preventing digital return currents from flowing through sensitive analog areas. Therefore, AGND and DGND do not necessarily need to be electrically isolated. What matters more is controlling the return-current path. (return-current path) Why Ground Plane Splitting Can Cause More Problems In traditional PCB layout, it is common to see analog and digital areas separated into AGND and DGND regions, with the two planes connected at a single point. It may look like a professional solution, but there is an important question: What happens to the return current when a digital signal crosses from the digital area into the analog area? For high-speed digital signals, return current tends to follow the lowest-impedance path in the reference plane and is concentrated near the area directly underneath the signal trace. If the ground plane is split, the return current can no longer follow a short path underneath the signal. Instead, it may have to travel around the split. As the return path becomes longer, the loop area increases and parasitic inductance can also increase. This may result in more EMI and crosstalk rather than less. Therefore, splitting the ground plane does not automatically reduce noise. In some cases, it can actually make signal integrity and EMI problems worse. This is especially important when a high-speed signal crosses a ground-plane split. The return current is forced to take a longer path, which can increase the loop area and introduce additional noise. For this reason, a good mixed-signal PCB design does not simply focus on physically separating analog and digital grounds. It focuses on keeping the return-current paths controlled and predictable. (AGND plane & DGND plane) Four Critical Return Paths in ADC PCB Layout For an ADC, the most important consideration is not simply whether the analog and digital grounds are physically separated. Instead, different types of return current should follow appropriate paths and avoid sensitive circuits whenever possible. 1. Analog Input Return The reference ground for the analog input should be located as close as practical to the ADC's AGND. Avoid allowing the analog input return current to travel through the MCU area or other high-noise digital regions. 2. ADC Power Return The return path from the AVDD decoupling capacitor should be kept short and should return to the analog ground near the ADC. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor depends not only on whether the capacitor is present, but also on the loop formed by the power pin, capacitor, and ground connection. Keeping this loop small is an important part of good ADC PCB layout . 3. Digital Interface Return High-speed transitions on SPI signals such as SCLK, MOSI, MISO, and CS can generate high-frequency transient currents. These return currents should form a compact loop near the digital interface whenever possible, rather than flowing through sensitive analog ground regions. 4. AGND/DGND Connection Inside the PCB Layout Regardless of how the PCB is partitioned, AGND and DGND ultimately need to return to the same system reference ground. Whether the connection should use a single-point connection, a local connection, or a continuous ground plane depends on the ADC/DAC manufacturer's datasheet and recommended PCB layout. So, what you really want to achieve is: Keep different types of return current on controlled paths rather than simply separating the two ground planes. Should You Use a Ferrite Bead Between AGND and DGND? This is one area where I would strongly recommend against blindly applying a common rule. A design like this is sometimes seen: AGND ─── Ferrite Bead ─── DGND The idea is that the ferrite bead can block digital noise from reaching the analog ground. In certain power-filtering applications, ferrite beads can indeed provide frequency-dependent impedance and help suppress high-frequency noise. However, ground is not simply a noise path. It is an important system reference and also provides return-current paths for signals. Once a frequency-dependent component is inserted between AGND and DGND, a voltage difference between the two ground domains can develop depending on the current and frequency. For high-precision ADCs and DACs, this ground potential difference can itself become a source of error or noise. Therefore, unless the device manufacturer specifically recommends it, do not add a ferrite bead between AGND and DGND simply because you have heard that analog and digital grounds should be isolated. Key AGND vs DGND Considerations for Mixed-Signal PCB Design In summary, AGND and DGND can often share the same ground reference, but the exact connection method should always follow the ADC/DAC manufacturer's datasheet and recommended PCB layout. When designing the board, pay particular attention to: Whether digital return current flows through sensitive analog areas Whether the analog input return path is short and well controlled Whether the ADC power-decoupling loop is compact Whether high-speed digital signals cross a ground-plane split Whether unnecessary impedance exists between AGND and DGND So, instead of simply thinking: "Analog ground must always be separated from digital ground." A more accurate way to think about AGND vs DGND is: The grounds can be shared, but the return currents should be controlled. The ground plane can remain continuous, but the paths taken by noise currents must be carefully managed. For ADCs, DACs, and other mixed-signal devices, good mixed-signal PCB design is not simply about physically isolating analog and digital ground. It is about using proper PCB layout, routing, decoupling, and return-path control to prevent digital noise from coupling into sensitive analog circuits. If a device has separate analog and digital ground pins, should they be connected directly, separated into different ground planes, or joined at a single point? This question is especially important in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design, where fast digital switching currents can potentially interfere with sensitive analog circuits. To understand the right approach to AGND vs DGND, the key is not simply whether the two grounds are connected, but how the return currents flow through the PCB. (schematic with AGND & GND) Why Do ADCs and DACs Have Separate AGND and DGND Pins? An ADC can be roughly understood as having two different domains. One side contains the sampling circuit, op amp, reference, comparator, PGA, DAC core, and analog bias circuits. These belong to the analog domain. The other side contains the SPI/I²C interface, digital logic, registers, clock, state machine, and other digital circuits. These belong to the digital domain. One of the biggest characteristics of digital circuits is that their current can change very quickly. For example, when an SPI interface operates at tens of MHz, every clock transition can generate transient current. These currents need to form a complete return path through the power and ground network. This is where the problem begins. Assume the digital return current is: ID = 50 mA and it flows through a PCB trace with only: R = 20 mΩ The resulting ground voltage variation is: V = IR = 50 mA × 20 mΩ = 1 mV. 1 mV may look very small, but it is not necessarily negligible for a high-resolution ADC. For example, consider a 16-bit ADC with a 2.5 V full-scale range: 1 LSB ≈ 2.5 V / 65536 ≈ 38.1 μV Therefore, a 1 mV ground voltage variation corresponds to approximately: 1 mV / 38.1 μV ≈ 26 LSB Of course, the actual ADC conversion error depends on how this ground disturbance couples into the analog input, reference, and internal circuits. However, this example illustrates an important point: For a high-precision ADC, the key concern is not simply how low the ground resistance is, but where the digital return current flows. This is one of the fundamental considerations in ADC PCB layout and mixed-signal PCB design. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected Directly? In many designs, AGND and DGND ultimately connect to the same ground reference. However, there is an important condition: this does not mean that AGND and DGND can simply be connected with two arbitrary traces and left at that. If the ADC or DAC datasheet specifies that AGND and DGND should be connected close to the device, follow the manufacturer's recommended layout. For many high-precision ADCs and DACs, the recommended PCB layout is designed to maintain a low-impedance, low-inductance connection between AGND and DGND while preventing digital return currents from flowing through sensitive analog areas. Therefore, AGND and DGND do not necessarily need to be electrically isolated. What matters more is controlling the return-current path. (return-current path) Why Ground Plane Splitting Can Cause More Problems In traditional PCB layout, it is common to see analog and digital areas separated into AGND and DGND regions, with the two planes connected at a single point. It may look like a professional solution, but there is an important question: What happens to the return current when a digital signal crosses from the digital area into the analog area? For high-speed digital signals, return current tends to follow the lowest-impedance path in the reference plane and is concentrated near the area directly underneath the signal trace. If the ground plane is split, the return current can no longer follow a short path underneath the signal. Instead, it may have to travel around the split. As the return path becomes longer, the loop area increases and parasitic inductance can also increase. This may result in more EMI and crosstalk rather than less. Therefore, splitting the ground plane does not automatically reduce noise. In some cases, it can actually make signal integrity and EMI problems worse. This is especially important when a high-speed signal crosses a ground-plane split. The return current is forced to take a longer path, which can increase the loop area and introduce additional noise. For this reason, a good mixed-signal PCB design does not simply focus on physically separating analog and digital grounds. It focuses on keeping the return-current paths controlled and predictable. (AGND plane & DGND plane) Four Critical Return Paths in ADC PCB Layout For an ADC, the most important consideration is not simply whether the analog and digital grounds are physically separated. Instead, different types of return current should follow appropriate paths and avoid sensitive circuits whenever possible. 1. Analog Input Return The reference ground for the analog input should be located as close as practical to the ADC's AGND. Avoid allowing the analog input return current to travel through the MCU area or other high-noise digital regions. 2. ADC Power Return The return path from the AVDD decoupling capacitor should be kept short and should return to the analog ground near the ADC. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor depends not only on whether the capacitor is present, but also on the loop formed by the power pin, capacitor, and ground connection. Keeping this loop small is an important part of good ADC PCB layout . 3. Digital Interface Return High-speed transitions on SPI signals such as SCLK, MOSI, MISO, and CS can generate high-frequency transient currents. These return currents should form a compact loop near the digital interface whenever possible, rather than flowing through sensitive analog ground regions. 4. AGND/DGND Connection Inside the PCB Layout Regardless of how the PCB is partitioned, AGND and DGND ultimately need to return to the same system reference ground. Whether the connection should use a single-point connection, a local connection, or a continuous ground plane depends on the ADC/DAC manufacturer's datasheet and recommended PCB layout. So, what you really want to achieve is: Keep different types of return current on controlled paths rather than simply separating the two ground planes. Should You Use a Ferrite Bead Between AGND and DGND? This is one area where I would strongly recommend against blindly applying a common rule. A design like this is sometimes seen: AGND ─── Ferrite Bead ─── DGND The idea is that the ferrite bead can block digital noise from reaching the analog ground. In certain power-filtering applications, ferrite beads can indeed provide frequency-dependent impedance and help suppress high-frequency noise. However, ground is not simply a noise path. It is an important system reference and also provides return-current paths for signals. Once a frequency-dependent component is inserted between AGND and DGND, a voltage difference between the two ground domains can develop depending on the current and frequency. For high-precision ADCs and DACs, this ground potential difference can itself become a source of error or noise. Therefore, unless the device manufacturer specifically recommends it, do not add a ferrite bead between AGND and DGND simply because you have heard that analog and digital grounds should be isolated. Key AGND vs DGND Considerations for Mixed-Signal PCB Design In summary, AGND and DGND can often share the same ground reference, but the exact connection method should always follow the ADC/DAC manufacturer's datasheet and recommended PCB layout. When designing the board, pay particular attention to: Whether digital return current flows through sensitive analog areas Whether the analog input return path is short and well controlled Whether the ADC power-decoupling loop is compact Whether high-speed digital signals cross a ground-plane split Whether unnecessary impedance exists between AGND and DGND So, instead of simply thinking: "Analog ground must always be separated from digital ground." A more accurate way to think about AGND vs DGND is: The grounds can be shared, but the return currents should be controlled. The ground plane can remain continuous, but the paths taken by noise currents must be carefully managed. For ADCs, DACs, and other mixed-signal devices, good mixed-signal PCB design is not simply about physically isolating analog and digital ground. It is about using proper PCB layout, routing, decoupling, and return-path control to prevent digital noise from coupling into sensitive analog circuits. Verify Now Blog > High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices by: Mila Sep 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout high speed analog to digital converter high speed adc adc layout adc pcb design High-speed analog-to-digital converter (ADC) PCB layout involves multiple design parameters, and their importance varies depending on the application. For high-speed ADC systems, the focus should not be on optimizing every routing detail, but on avoiding common design deviations and maintaining the overall performance of the signal chain. For a broader overview of PCB Layout principles, designers should also consider signal integrity, power integrity, grounding, and return paths as part of the overall design. 1. EPAD Design Guidelines for ADC PCB Design The exposed pad (EPAD), defined as Pin 0 by ADI, is the core pad located on the bottom of many integrated circuit packages. It typically provides the main grounding and thermal connection and serves as an important path for the internal ground structure. Some converters and amplifiers do not have dedicated ground pins, with their grounding function primarily relying on the EPAD. Therefore, EPAD design directly affects electrical connection stability and thermal performance and should not be overlooked in ADC PCB design. The EPAD must form a reliable solder connection with the PCB to ensure both electrical and thermal connectivity. Poor soldering or insufficient contact can lead to abnormal grounding, inadequate heat dissipation, and even malfunction of the signal chain. For reliable EPAD performance, three key aspects should be considered in ADC PCB design. Multilayer Grounding and Thermal Copper According to the device datasheet and overall thermal requirements, grounding and thermal copper structures can be added on the appropriate PCB layers. These structures should provide reliable electrical and thermal connections to the PCB ground planes, helping improve heat dissipation, particularly in high-power and multichannel signal-chain applications. The bottom layer can also incorporate a corresponding grounding or thermal area when required by the device and system design. Depending on the application, this area can support grounding, thermal management, high-frequency decoupling, or mechanical positioning for a bottom-side thermal structure. （exposed pad pcb design） EPAD Pad Segmentation A large EPAD can be divided into multiple smaller areas using a cross-hatched stencil pattern or solder mask segmentation. During reflow soldering, solder paste distribution can vary across a large continuous pad, potentially resulting in uneven soldering, voids, or insufficient effective contact. Proper EPAD segmentation helps improve solder paste distribution and create a more uniform and stable connection between the device and PCB, improving both electrical and thermal reliability. EPAD Ground Vias and Via Filling Ground vias can be added to individual EPAD sections according to the device recommendations and PCB manufacturing requirements. Whether these vias require solder paste filling, epoxy filling, or other treatment depends on the via dimensions, pad structure, and manufacturing process. For via structures that may allow solder paste to flow into the holes during reflow, appropriate via filling or solder mask treatment should be considered. This helps reduce soldering defects and improves the reliability of the EPAD electrical and thermal connection. (EPAD design: large vs segmented) 2. Power Decoupling and PDS Design for High-Speed ADC The primary goal of PCB power decoupling is to reduce the impedance of the power delivery system (PDS) to ground. A common mistake is to place large numbers of capacitors with different capacitance values without considering their actual frequency response. In practice, a large number of redundant capacitors is not always necessary. Carefully selecting capacitors based on capacitance, component type, package, and process characteristics can optimize PDS impedance while saving PCB space and reducing component cost. Redundant capacitors can introduce layout congestion, additional cost, and potential resonance risks. They do not inherently violate PCB manufacturing requirements, but excessive or poorly planned decoupling can reduce overall design efficiency. Capacitor Selection and PCB Decoupling Layout The performance of a capacitor varies with its package and construction. Even capacitors from the same supplier can have different frequency responses depending on package size, process, and component type. Therefore, there is no universal frequency limit for capacitor decoupling performance. The effective frequency range depends on package size, equivalent series inductance (ESL), component characteristics, and the actual PCB layout. If capacitor selection or placement is inappropriate, multiple capacitors can introduce additional inductive loops. Capacitors with different parameters may also resonate at specific frequencies, potentially increasing rather than reducing PDS impedance. Capacitor frequency-response characteristics should therefore be considered before placement and selection. （ADC decoupling capacitor layout） 3. High-Frequency PDS and PCB Stackup Design The effective decoupling range of discrete capacitors depends on their electrical characteristics and PCB layout, and there is no universal high-frequency cutoff. As frequency increases, package parasitics and ESL increasingly limit the high-frequency performance of discrete capacitors. At higher frequencies, the intrinsic capacitance formed between PCB power and ground planes becomes an important part of PDS design. Proper stackup design can therefore complement conventional discrete decoupling. Six-Layer PCB Stackup A typical six-layer PCB stackup can be arranged as: Top Signal → Ground 1 → Power 1 → Power 2 → Ground 2 → Bottom Signal In high-speed PCB design, keeping the dielectric thickness between adjacent power and ground planes relatively small, such as a typical range of 2–4 mil, helps increase plane capacitance and reduce the impedance of high-frequency current paths. This optimization is achieved primarily through the PCB stackup and does not require additional components. The required stackup and dielectric thickness simply need to be specified in the PCB fabrication documentation. Eight-Layer PCB Stackup Optimization For an eight-layer PCB, additional ground reference layers can be introduced while maintaining a small core-layer spacing, such as 2–3 mil. This can significantly increase the intrinsic plane capacitance, although the actual increase is not necessarily double. It depends on dielectric thickness, copper area, and the overall configuration of the power and ground layers. Compared with simply adding more high-frequency discrete capacitors, stackup optimization can reduce component count and provide a cleaner high-frequency PDS structure. PDS Impedance and Dynamic Current The primary function of the PDS is to suppress voltage fluctuations caused by the dynamic current demand of the circuit. Low-impedance power and ground planes, combined with an appropriate PCB stackup, can reduce voltage fluctuations caused by rapidly changing currents. According to V = IR, if the dynamic current is 1 A and the PDS impedance is 10 mΩ, the corresponding voltage variation is approximately 10 mV. Optimizing the PCB stackup can extend the effective high-frequency low-impedance range, but overall PDS performance is also affected by power-plane integrity, ground-via placement, package parasitics, and local current-loop design. Therefore, conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can be placed at key locations such as power-entry points, high-power devices, and surge-current devices. Combining different decoupling mechanisms can help optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. Dense capacitor placement around every IC is not always necessary and may introduce unnecessary cost, space consumption, and resonance risks. （discrete vs plane capacitance） 4. PCB Layer-to-Layer Coupling and Noise Suppression In multilayer PCB layouts, sensitive analog layers, including analog power, ground, and signal layers, can experience crosstalk when placed close to high-frequency digital layers. Because some noise sources are located directly above or below sensitive analog layers, this type of coupling can easily be overlooked. Layer Coupling in ADC Layout Adjacent PCB conductor layers form parasitic capacitive structures, which can produce electric-field coupling under certain frequency and layout conditions. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. By addressing these factors together, designers can improve the stability and overall performance of high-speed ADC systems. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Dense capacitor placement around every IC is not always necessary and may introduce unnecessary cost, space consumption, and resonance risks. （discrete vs plane capacitance） 4. PCB Layer-to-Layer Coupling and Noise Suppression In multilayer PCB layouts, sensitive analog layers, including analog power, ground, and signal layers, can experience crosstalk when placed close to high-frequency digital layers. Because some noise sources are located directly above or below sensitive analog layers, this type of coupling can easily be overlooked. Layer Coupling in ADC Layout Adjacent PCB conductor layers form parasitic capacitive structures, which can produce electric-field coupling under certain frequency and layout conditions. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. By addressing these factors together, designers can improve the stability and overall performance of high-speed ADC systems. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design by: Mila Sep 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout schematic design cmos pins nc pins When working on schematic design , engineers often encounter situations like this: to meet the core functional requirements, a 100-pin MCU is selected, but only 60 pins are actually used. Or a 4-channel op-amp is selected, but only three channels are needed. Some ICs may also have pins marked as NC. Seeing all those pins labeled as "Not Connected" on the schematic can be confusing. Should these unused pins simply be left floating? Should they be connected to ground? Or should they be connected to a power supply? Improper handling of unused pins can lead to undefined input states, increased power consumption, or noise interference, and in severe cases may even affect device reliability. This article explains how to properly handle these seemingly minor but important details in schematic design. 1. Why Should Unused IC Pins Be Handled Carefully? Many ICs today use CMOS technology. One key rule to remember is: do not leave CMOS inputs floating, especially digital input pins. （CMOS device） This can be understood from the internal structure of CMOS circuits. A typical CMOS input stage consists of an inverter made up of a PMOS and an NMOS connected in series. When the input is low, the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off. When the input is high, the PMOS is off and the NMOS is on. Under ideal static conditions, only a very small leakage current flows, giving CMOS circuits very low static power consumption. 2. What Happens When CMOS Pins Are Left Floating? What happens when an input is left floating? Because the input has very high impedance, it can easily be affected by surrounding electromagnetic noise, parasitic coupling, and leakage current. As a result, the input voltage may become undefined and fluctuate between low and high levels. When the input voltage falls within the transition region of the CMOS input stage, the PMOS and NMOS may both be partially turned on, causing increased supply current. In other words, floating CMOS pins have no guaranteed logic state, so it is impossible to reliably determine whether the input will be interpreted as a high or low level. 3. How to Handle Unused MCU GPIOs? Modern MCUs usually provide multifunctional GPIOs. For unused GPIOs, follow the requirements in the device datasheet and configure the corresponding IO as an output with a defined state, such as driving it low or high. If supported by the device, it can also be configured as an input with an internal pull-up or pull-down. When permitted by the device, this eliminates the need for external pull-up or pull-down resistors, saving components and PCB space. For critical pins such as interrupt, reset, and mode-selection pins, however, their default logic states should be clearly defined. Whether an external pull-up or pull-down resistor is required should be determined according to the datasheet and reference design to prevent unintended triggering. 4. How to Handle Unused Op-Amp Channels? Op-amps and ADCs require special attention because analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, and their unused pins may need to be handled differently from digital circuits. For example, if you use a dual-channel op-amp but only need one channel, what should you do with the unused channel? （IC Pins） Leaving it floating is generally not recommended because the input pins can pick up noise, causing the output to saturate and potentially increasing power consumption. What if both the non-inverting and inverting inputs are connected to ground? This puts the op-amp in an open-loop configuration, so its output may not be well controlled. For a typical voltage-feedback op-amp, if permitted by the datasheet, a better approach is to configure the unused channel as a voltage follower: connect the output to the inverting input to create negative feedback, and connect the non-inverting input to GND. However, the op-amp's input common-mode range and output swing must also be checked to ensure that this configuration is within the device's specifications. 5. What About Unused ADC Inputs? Unused ADC channels should be handled according to the device datasheet. Some devices recommend connecting unused ADC inputs to GND or another stable reference level to prevent the channel from picking up noise. However, directly connecting the input to ground should not be treated as a universal rule for all ADCs. Therefore, unused ADC inputs should not simply be treated in the same way as digital GPIOs. Always check the manufacturer's recommended connection method before finalizing the schematic design. 6. What Do NC Pins Mean on an IC? IC datasheets often contain pins marked as NC, or "No Connect." These NC pins need to be examined carefully. NC does not necessarily mean that the pin can be connected in any way. Some NC pins may have no internal connection and should simply be left floating. However, other pins marked as NC may have internal connections related to testing, reserved functions, or other circuits. The handling method must strictly follow the datasheet. For example, some datasheets specify "Must be left floating," while others specify "Must be tied to GND." If you connect NC pins to ground without checking the datasheet, you could potentially cause unexpected behavior or interfere with internal test or reserved functions. 7. The Key Rule: Always Check the Datasheet When dealing with unused IC pins, the most important principle is not simply whether a pin should be left floating or connected to ground. Instead, first identify the pin type and then follow the connection requirements specified in the datasheet. （DBV package） Different types of GPIOs, analog inputs, op-amp channels, and NC pins may require completely different handling methods. In simple terms: Unused GPIOs: Configure them to a defined state according to the datasheet. Critical input pins: Make sure they have a clearly defined default logic level. Unused op-amp channels: Use a stable negative-feedback configuration when recommended. Unused ADC inputs: Follow the device manufacturer's recommended connection method. NC pins: Strictly follow the datasheet requirements. A simple "Not Connected" label on a schematic may involve power consumption, noise, stability, and even device reliability. Do not rely on assumptions. Check the datasheet first, then decide how the pin should be connected. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide by: Mila Sep 08,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hardware design type c design usb design usb type c design usb pcb design One of the most common pitfalls in Hardware Design for Type-C interfaces is confusing the legacy protocols used by USB-A ports with the native USB Type-C protocol. Some designers mistakenly treat D+ / D− as the core charging detection pins of Type-C, which can lead to design failures. The voltage is a normal 5V, the polarity is correct, but the device still does not charge, fails to be recognized, only works in one plug orientation, or has limited charging current. Compatibility issues may also occur with some phones. In many cases, there is basically one reason: CC1 and CC2 are not connected correctly. Let's look at the most common 5V Type-C charging configuration. Once you understand it, you can use it directly in your Type C Design. 1. The Most Important Conclusion For a Type-C interface, CC1 / CC2 are the core channels for power role detection, connection detection, current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ and D− do not handle basic Type-C power detection or USB PD negotiation in a standard C-to-C connection. This is one of the key differences between traditional USB and modern USB Type C Design: CC pins: The dedicated Type-C configuration channel used for power role detection, connection detection, plug orientation detection, Type-C current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ / D− pins: Mainly used for USB 2.0 data transmission and compatibility with certain legacy charging protocols, such as BC1.2. In simple terms: C-to-C charging: Basic power detection mainly relies on CC, not D+ / D−. A-to-C charging: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may use D+ / D− for charging detection. 2. Why Does C-to-C Charging Mainly Rely on CC? Taking a standard USB-C-to-USB-C charging connection as an example, the Source and Sink first establish a connection through the CC pins. The basic process is: 1. The charger provides Rp pull-ups on CC1 and CC2. 2. The phone or other powered device uses Rd pull-downs to indicate that it is a Sink. 3. The two sides detect the connection and determine the available Type-C current capability through CC. 4. If both sides support USB PD, they can further communicate through the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. It is important to note that 56KΩ, 22KΩ, and 10KΩ Rp values correspond to different advertised current capabilities. They should not be interpreted as “56KΩ directly unlocks 5V/3A.” Therefore, Type-C current capability detection and USB PD fast charging should be distinguished: Type-C current capability detection → Rp / Rd USB PD power negotiation → PD communication over CC D+ / D− mainly handle USB 2.0 data and certain legacy charging protocols. 3. CC vs. D+ / D−: What Does Each One Actually Do? CC1 / CC2: The Core Type-C Power and Connection Pins CC stands for Configuration Channel and is an important feature that distinguishes USB Type-C from traditional USB-A interfaces. CC1 and CC2 are mainly responsible for: Power role detection: Rp indicates a Source, while Rd indicates a Sink. Connection detection: Determines whether a valid connection has been established. Plug orientation detection: The active CC pin helps determine the plug orientation. Type-C current capability detection: The Source uses Rp to advertise its power capability. USB PD communication: USB PD devices use the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. Therefore, in a standard Type-C C-to-C power connection: Correct CC configuration is critical to proper device detection and power delivery. This is why CC routing and component placement are important in USB PCB Design. D+ / D−: Data Transmission and Legacy Charging Compatibility D+ / D− are essentially USB 2.0 differential data lines. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−. The key distinction is: C-to-C architecture: Basic Type-C power detection relies on CC. A-to-C architecture: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may involve D+ / D−. Therefore, the fact that D+ / D− were widely used for charging detection in the USB-A era does not mean that they are required for basic charging in a USB-C-to-USB-C connection. This distinction is important in practical USB Design . 4. Three Common CC Configurations + Applicable Scenarios The most common Type-C CC configurations can be divided into three categories: Sink, Source, and DRP. Typical resistor values include: Rp = 56KΩ / 22KΩ / 10KΩ Rd = 5.1KΩ The exact configuration depends on the device role and the Type-C / USB PD requirements. Configuration 1: Dual 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → 5.1KΩ → GND CC2 → 5.1KΩ → GND Applicable to: Phones, development boards, microcontroller boards, small appliances, and other Type-C devices that work as Sink devices. Function: The device indicates that it is a powered device, allowing the Source to detect the connection and determine the plug orientation. For basic Type-C power, this configuration can support standard 5V operation. Note: Two 5.1KΩ resistors do not automatically give the device USB PD fast-charging capability. PCB Conformal Coating: Which Components Need Masking? by: Mila Sep 23,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB conformal coating Applying a conformal coating to the PCB during PCB assembly process can enhance the PCB's resistance to moisture, salt spray, dust, and corrosive environments. However, it is essentially an insulating protective film. For this reason, not every area of a PCB is suitable for direct coating. Areas that require electrical contact, mechanical movement, heat dissipation, or optical transmission can actually develop new reliability issues if they are improperly coated. Especially for the following components, applying conformal coating directly without proper masking can lead to a situation where the PCB has been coated for protection, but the product develops problems because critical areas were coated when they should not have been. So, let’s take a closer look at where PCB conformal coating needs special attention. 1. Connectors: Protect Electrical Contact Areas Connectors are usually one of the most important components to keep clear of conformal coating. The reason is simple: their contacts need to maintain reliable electrical contact. For example, if a connector contact normally has a contact resistance of only a few tens of mΩ, allowing conformal coating to enter the contact area essentially adds an insulating film between the mating surfaces. The problem can be even more complicated because some connectors may still work after the first few mating cycles, as the coating can be scraped away from the contact area. But that does not mean the connection will remain reliable. Over time, vibration, temperature and humidity cycling, coating residue, contamination, and oxidation of the contact surface can all increase contact resistance or cause intermittent contact. In actual PCB conformal coating applications, the electrical contact area, mating area, and other surfaces that must maintain reliable contact generally need to be masked. The exact masking area should be determined according to the connector manufacturer's coating requirements. This is especially important in automotive electronics and industrial control equipment that operate under long-term vibration. Being able to conduct electricity once does not necessarily mean the connection will remain reliable. （Connectors component） 2. Relays and Switches: Keep Contacts and Moving Parts Clear Contacts and moving mechanisms also require special attention, making relays another type of component that needs careful consideration during conformal coating. A relay typically contains contacts, an armature, springs, and other mechanical structures. If conformal coating enters the moving mechanism, it may affect the mechanical action of the relay. More importantly, the contacts themselves are critical because a relay relies on mechanical contacts to make and break an electrical circuit. If the contact surfaces are contaminated by coating, contact resistance, arcing characteristics, and long-term reliability may all be affected. Therefore, it does not mean that the entire relay must always be left uncoated. For sealed relays that have been verified as compatible with conformal coating, the outside of the component and the surrounding PCB may still be coated for protection. The areas that require particular attention are the contacts, moving mechanisms, and any areas specifically designated as coating-prohibited by the manufacturer. For high-voltage relays, additional considerations include creepage distance, clearance, and the effect of the coating on insulation performance. It should not simply be assumed that conformal coating automatically provides sufficient electrical isolation. 3. Buttons and Potentiometers: Avoid Coating Moving Contacts Components that contain moving or contacting mechanisms also require special attention. Mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components can be affected if conformal coating enters their internal moving or contact areas. For example, a potentiometer contains sliding contacts. If conformal coating penetrates into the mechanism, it can form a thin insulating contamination layer over the sliding contacts. What can happen? Resistance jumps, poor contact, and increased noise are all possible. This can be particularly troublesome in analog circuits because the problem may not appear as an obvious component failure. Instead, it may show up as increased output noise, ADC reading drift, or other intermittent problems that are difficult to trace. Therefore, for mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components, the masking area should be determined based on the component structure and manufacturer's requirements rather than simply applying full-component coating. （Buttons component） 4. Power Components: Consider Thermal Performance MOSFETs, DC-DC converters, LDOs, and other power components often have large copper areas around them to help dissipate heat. The effect of conformal coating on thermal performance cannot simply be described as "coating always causes the temperature to increase by a certain amount." Instead, the entire thermal path needs to be considered. For power components that rely on PCB copper, thermal vias, thermal pads, or external heat sinks for heat dissipation, the coating location, coating thickness, and overall mechanical design may all affect the final thermal performance. For example, assume a power component dissipates 2 W and its junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is 30 °C/W. Under this simplified model, the temperature rise is approximately: ΔT = P × θJA = 2 × 30 = 60 °C If the overall thermal conditions cause the effective thermal resistance to increase to 40 °C/W: ΔT = 2 × 40 = 80 °C Under this assumption, the temperature rise increases by 20 °C. It is important to note that this is only a simplified example showing how changes in thermal resistance affect temperature rise. It does not mean that conformal coating itself will necessarily increase θJA from 30 °C/W to 40 °C/W. The actual result depends on factors such as PCB copper area, thermal vias, component package, airflow, heat sink design, coating material, and coating thickness. Therefore, for high-power MOSFETs, power inductors, rectifier diodes, DC-DC converters, and similar components, the key question is whether the overall thermal path becomes less effective after coating. For thermal pads, thermal vias, exposed heat-dissipation surfaces, and areas that contact a heat sink, the need for masking should be determined based on the component and mechanical design rather than coating everything simply to achieve complete coverage. 5. Optical Components: Protect Optical Paths Conformal coating can also directly affect the performance of optical components. LEDs, photoelectric sensors, infrared receivers, cameras, light-sensitive devices, and similar components require particular attention. Conformal coating can change the transmittance, reflectivity, or surface condition of an optical window. For example, if a photoelectric sensor is calibrated for a specific optical window and an additional coating layer is applied to that surface, the optical path may change. As a result, sensors in the same production batch may produce inconsistent outputs. For components involving an optical path, first confirm with the component manufacturer whether conformal coating is permitted and what materials, coating thicknesses, and coverage areas are allowed. Do not assume that a coating will have no optical impact simply because the coating itself is transparent. 6. PCB Conformal Coating Is Not About Complete Coverage One of the most common mistakes in PCB conformal coating is treating complete coverage as the ultimate goal. A better approach is simple: protect the areas that need protection, and keep critical areas free of coating. During the PCB design stage, the coating requirements for different areas should be defined in advance. In general, they can be considered in three categories: Areas That Should Be Coated Exposed copper Solder joints General passive components and their soldered areas Areas that are vulnerable to moisture, salt spray, and corrosion Areas That Should Be Kept Free of Coating or Masked Electrical contact areas of connectors Moving or contacting mechanisms in buttons and potentiometers Test points Optical windows Other areas that need to maintain electrical or mechanical contact Components That Require Specification-Based Evaluation Power components Relays Transformers Sensors Crystals and oscillators Other specialized components The third category should not simply be classified as "coat" or "do not coat." The decision should be based on the component manufacturer's datasheet, coating compatibility, and the actual application environment. 7. How to Define Conformal Coating Areas During PCB Design Conformal coating should not be considered only after the PCB has been manufactured. The design stage should clearly define which areas require coating, which areas require masking, and what coating requirements need to be met. Coating Area Areas that require protection from moisture, contamination, corrosion, or other environmental factors. Keep-Out Area Areas that must remain free of conformal coating, such as connector contacts, test points, and optical windows. Masking Area Areas that need to be protected during manufacturing using masking tape, fixtures, or other masking methods. Thickness Requirement The target thickness of the conformal coating should be specified according to the application and material requirements. Inspection Requirement Quality requirements should be defined for coating coverage, missed coating, runs, bubbles, and other appearance or process-related defects. If you are sending your design for PCB production , it is recommended to clearly indicate the required coating and masking areas in the Gerber files, assembly drawings, or other production documentation. Conclusion Finally, do not rely only on the conformal coating manufacturer's documentation. The coating requirements of individual component manufacturers also need to be considered. For example, some connectors may allow coating while others explicitly prohibit it. Likewise, some MOSFETs may tolerate full coating, while others have thermal structures that require special treatment. Good PCB conformal coating design is not simply about maximizing coverage or increasing coating thickness. It is about clearly defining where coating should be applied, where it should not be applied, and why. The purpose of conformal coating is to improve PCB reliability in harsh environments, not to make the entire board look completely covered. By defining the Coating Area, Keep-Out Area, and Masking Area during the PCB design stage, the coating process and subsequent quality control can be much clearer and more reliable.
