PCB Conformal Coating: Which Components Need Masking? by: Mila Sep 23,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB conformal coating Applying a conformal coating to the PCB during PCB assembly process can enhance the PCB's resistance to moisture, salt spray, dust, and corrosive environments. However, it is essentially an insulating protective film. For this reason, not every area of a PCB is suitable for direct coating. Areas that require electrical contact, mechanical movement, heat dissipation, or optical transmission can actually develop new reliability issues if they are improperly coated. Especially for the following components, applying conformal coating directly without proper masking can lead to a situation where the PCB has been coated for protection, but the product develops problems because critical areas were coated when they should not have been. So, let’s take a closer look at where PCB conformal coating needs special attention. 1. Connectors: Protect Electrical Contact Areas Connectors are usually one of the most important components to keep clear of conformal coating. The reason is simple: their contacts need to maintain reliable electrical contact. For example, if a connector contact normally has a contact resistance of only a few tens of mΩ, allowing conformal coating to enter the contact area essentially adds an insulating film between the mating surfaces. The problem can be even more complicated because some connectors may still work after the first few mating cycles, as the coating can be scraped away from the contact area. But that does not mean the connection will remain reliable. Over time, vibration, temperature and humidity cycling, coating residue, contamination, and oxidation of the contact surface can all increase contact resistance or cause intermittent contact. In actual PCB conformal coating applications, the electrical contact area, mating area, and other surfaces that must maintain reliable contact generally need to be masked. The exact masking area should be determined according to the connector manufacturer's coating requirements. This is especially important in automotive electronics and industrial control equipment that operate under long-term vibration. Being able to conduct electricity once does not necessarily mean the connection will remain reliable. （Connectors component） 2. Relays and Switches: Keep Contacts and Moving Parts Clear Contacts and moving mechanisms also require special attention, making relays another type of component that needs careful consideration during conformal coating. A relay typically contains contacts, an armature, springs, and other mechanical structures. If conformal coating enters the moving mechanism, it may affect the mechanical action of the relay. More importantly, the contacts themselves are critical because a relay relies on mechanical contacts to make and break an electrical circuit. If the contact surfaces are contaminated by coating, contact resistance, arcing characteristics, and long-term reliability may all be affected. Therefore, it does not mean that the entire relay must always be left uncoated. For sealed relays that have been verified as compatible with conformal coating, the outside of the component and the surrounding PCB may still be coated for protection. The areas that require particular attention are the contacts, moving mechanisms, and any areas specifically designated as coating-prohibited by the manufacturer. For high-voltage relays, additional considerations include creepage distance, clearance, and the effect of the coating on insulation performance. It should not simply be assumed that conformal coating automatically provides sufficient electrical isolation. 3. Buttons and Potentiometers: Avoid Coating Moving Contacts Components that contain moving or contacting mechanisms also require special attention. Mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components can be affected if conformal coating enters their internal moving or contact areas. For example, a potentiometer contains sliding contacts. If conformal coating penetrates into the mechanism, it can form a thin insulating contamination layer over the sliding contacts. What can happen? Resistance jumps, poor contact, and increased noise are all possible. This can be particularly troublesome in analog circuits because the problem may not appear as an obvious component failure. Instead, it may show up as increased output noise, ADC reading drift, or other intermittent problems that are difficult to trace. Therefore, for mechanical buttons, potentiometers, DIP switches, and similar components, the masking area should be determined based on the component structure and manufacturer's requirements rather than simply applying full-component coating. （Buttons component） 4. Power Components: Consider Thermal Performance MOSFETs, DC-DC converters, LDOs, and other power components often have large copper areas around them to help dissipate heat. The effect of conformal coating on thermal performance cannot simply be described as "coating always causes the temperature to increase by a certain amount." Instead, the entire thermal path needs to be considered. For power components that rely on PCB copper, thermal vias, thermal pads, or external heat sinks for heat dissipation, the coating location, coating thickness, and overall mechanical design may all affect the final thermal performance. For example, assume a power component dissipates 2 W and its junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is 30 °C/W. Under this simplified model, the temperature rise is approximately: ΔT = P × θJA = 2 × 30 = 60 °C If the overall thermal conditions cause the effective thermal resistance to increase to 40 °C/W: ΔT = 2 × 40 = 80 °C Under this assumption, the temperature rise increases by 20 °C. It is important to note that this is only a simplified example showing how changes in thermal resistance affect temperature rise. It does not mean that conformal coating itself will necessarily increase θJA from 30 °C/W to 40 °C/W. The actual result depends on factors such as PCB copper area, thermal vias, component package, airflow, heat sink design, coating material, and coating thickness. Therefore, for high-power MOSFETs, power inductors, rectifier diodes, DC-DC converters, and similar components, the key question is whether the overall thermal path becomes less effective after coating. For thermal pads, thermal vias, exposed heat-dissipation surfaces, and areas that contact a heat sink, the need for masking should be determined based on the component and mechanical design rather than coating everything simply to achieve complete coverage. 5. Optical Components: Protect Optical Paths Conformal coating can also directly affect the performance of optical components. LEDs, photoelectric sensors, infrared receivers, cameras, light-sensitive devices, and similar components require particular attention. Conformal coating can change the transmittance, reflectivity, or surface condition of an optical window. For example, if a photoelectric sensor is calibrated for a specific optical window and an additional coating layer is applied to that surface, the optical path may change. As a result, sensors in the same production batch may produce inconsistent outputs. For components involving an optical path, first confirm with the component manufacturer whether conformal coating is permitted and what materials, coating thicknesses, and coverage areas are allowed. Do not assume that a coating will have no optical impact simply because the coating itself is transparent. 6. PCB Conformal Coating Is Not About Complete Coverage One of the most common mistakes in PCB conformal coating is treating complete coverage as the ultimate goal. A better approach is simple: protect the areas that need protection, and keep critical areas free of coating. During the PCB design stage, the coating requirements for different areas should be defined in advance. In general, they can be considered in three categories: Areas That Should Be Coated Exposed copper Solder joints General passive components and their soldered areas Areas that are vulnerable to moisture, salt spray, and corrosion Areas That Should Be Kept Free of Coating or Masked Electrical contact areas of connectors Moving or contacting mechanisms in buttons and potentiometers Test points Optical windows Other areas that need to maintain electrical or mechanical contact Components That Require Specification-Based Evaluation Power components Relays Transformers Sensors Crystals and oscillators Other specialized components The third category should not simply be classified as "coat" or "do not coat." The decision should be based on the component manufacturer's datasheet, coating compatibility, and the actual application environment. 7. How to Define Conformal Coating Areas During PCB Design Conformal coating should not be considered only after the PCB has been manufactured. The design stage should clearly define which areas require coating, which areas require masking, and what coating requirements need to be met. Coating Area Areas that require protection from moisture, contamination, corrosion, or other environmental factors. Keep-Out Area Areas that must remain free of conformal coating, such as connector contacts, test points, and optical windows. Masking Area Areas that need to be protected during manufacturing using masking tape, fixtures, or other masking methods. Thickness Requirement The target thickness of the conformal coating should be specified according to the application and material requirements. Inspection Requirement Quality requirements should be defined for coating coverage, missed coating, runs, bubbles, and other appearance or process-related defects. If you are sending your design for PCB production , it is recommended to clearly indicate the required coating and masking areas in the Gerber files, assembly drawings, or other production documentation. Conclusion Finally, do not rely only on the conformal coating manufacturer's documentation. The coating requirements of individual component manufacturers also need to be considered. For example, some connectors may allow coating while others explicitly prohibit it. Likewise, some MOSFETs may tolerate full coating, while others have thermal structures that require special treatment. Good PCB conformal coating design is not simply about maximizing coverage or increasing coating thickness. It is about clearly defining where coating should be applied, where it should not be applied, and why. The purpose of conformal coating is to improve PCB reliability in harsh environments, not to make the entire board look completely covered. By defining the Coating Area, Keep-Out Area, and Masking Area during the PCB design stage, the coating process and subsequent quality control can be much clearer and more reliable. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. PCB Layout Examples: From high-speed and RF to HDI, BGA, and rigid-flex designs, we handle a wide range of complex PCB layout requirements. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement by: Mila Sep 11,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout interface driver PCB connector placement interface PCB design People who design PCBs for embedded, industrial control, and communication hardware have probably heard a common PCB layout rule: interface drivers should be placed as close as possible to board-edge connectors. This is a practical guideline rather than an absolute requirement. For CAN and RS485, a slightly longer path may not immediately cause problems, while for high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe, longer traces can increase impedance discontinuities, parasitic effects, and return-path issues. If the driver is placed deep inside the board with a long trace between it and the connector, problems such as excessive radiated emissions, ESD-related MCU resets, closed high-speed eye diagrams, or communication errors may occur. This is why PCB connector placement and interface driver placement should be considered together in an interface PCB design . （Driver far from connector vs Driver close to connector ） 1. Three Common Types of Interface Drivers Interface drivers handle signal conversion and driving between the main controller on the PCB and external cables. Different interfaces have different transmission speeds, electrical standards, and communication protocols. From a functional perspective, they can be divided into three main categories. Level Translators / Interface Transceivers These devices primarily perform level conversion and interface adaptation, allowing two electrically incompatible systems on the PCB and external side to communicate correctly. RS232 transceiver (MAX232): Uses an internal charge pump to generate the positive and negative voltages required by RS-232. It converts TTL/CMOS logic levels on the MCU side into RS-232 levels, while the receiver performs the reverse conversion. RS-232 is a single-ended interface referenced to signal ground, not a differential interface. RS485/RS422 transceiver (MAX485): Converts single-ended TTL signals into differential signals and provides the drive capability required for long-distance bus transmission. CAN transceiver (TJA1050): Handles level conversion between the MCU logic side and the CAN bus, and drives and receives bus signals according to the dominant and recessive states defined by CAN. A practical CAN interface normally also requires external protection devices such as TVS diodes. High-Speed Physical Layer / PHY PHY devices for USB, Ethernet, HDMI/DisplayPort, and other high-speed interfaces integrate physical-layer functions for signal transmission and reception, including functions such as equalization and swing control. From a PCB layout perspective, controlled impedance, continuous reference planes, and an appropriate routing topology are required to maintain signal integrity. Differential impedance, such as 90Ω or 100Ω, is primarily determined by trace width, trace spacing, dielectric thickness, dielectric constant, and the reference plane. These parameters are implemented through the PCB stackup and routing design rather than being determined by the PHY itself. Differential Interface Drivers / Receivers Differential drivers and receivers such as LVDS and CML devices are used for high-speed point-to-point transmission. They precisely control differential common-mode voltage and signal swing to reduce jitter and overshoot during high-speed transmission. 2. Why Should Interface Drivers Usually Be Placed Close to Board-Edge Connectors? The following four factors apply differently depending on the interface type and should be evaluated as part of the overall interface PCB design. Shorten the Boundary Trace and Reduce EMI and ESD Risks Long traces between a connector and its driver increase the distance over which high-speed signals travel across the PCB and may increase the effective loop area of high-frequency currents. When the reference plane is discontinuous or the return path is interrupted, these traces are more likely to generate common-mode currents and additional EMI radiation. External ESD, surges, and environmental interference may also couple into the board through these paths. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens this section of the trace and reduces the high-frequency loop area, helping to lower the risk of radiated emissions and internal interference coupling. This can also reduce the workload during EMC debugging. However, EMI risk is not determined by trace length alone. Return paths, reference planes, loop area, signal edge rate, common-mode current, connector structure, and cable coupling all play important roles in PCB layout. Reduce Parasitic Effects and Maintain High-Speed Signal Integrity PCB traces inherently have parasitic capacitance and inductance. For high-speed differential interfaces such as USB, PCIe, MIPI, and HDMI, longer traces can increase the accumulated parasitic effects and make it more difficult to maintain impedance continuity. This can lead to slower signal edges, overshoot, ringing, and reflections, resulting in eye closure and increased bit error rates. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens the signal path, reduces unnecessary parasitic effects, and simplifies the routing topology, making it easier to maintain a continuous controlled-impedance transmission path. This is particularly important in high-speed interface PCB design. Shorten the ESD Discharge Path and Improve Protection Effectiveness Serial ports, Ethernet ports, and HDMI connectors are common entry points for ESD and surge energy. The effectiveness of ESD protection depends on many factors, including the type and location of the TVS device, dynamic clamping voltage, discharge path, grounding structure, PCB stackup, MCU tolerance, and interface isolation. It is therefore not determined by trace length alone. Placing the driver and ESD protection devices close to the connector and connecting them to the ground plane with short, direct traces helps provide a low-impedance discharge path. This reduces the risk of high-voltage pulses coupling into the core circuitry. During ESD testing, a system may experience MCU resets, communication errors, or, in severe cases, component damage. These problems need to be addressed through the overall protection architecture rather than relying on connector placement alone. Maintain a Continuous Path Between the Transceiver and Connector For differential interfaces such as RS485 and CAN, the relatively small signal swing makes differential transmission an important part of their noise immunity. Rather than simply assuming that the signal will experience significant amplitude loss along a long PCB trace, it is more important to consider whether the path between the transceiver and connector is short, continuous, and supported by a clear return path. Excessive trace length, too many vias, branches, and impedance discontinuities can increase parasitic effects and reflections while also increasing the possibility of external noise coupling into the signal path. Therefore, as part of good PCB connector placement, the differential path between the transceiver and connector should generally be kept as short and continuous as practical. 3. Practical PCB Layout Guidelines for Interface Circuit Guideline 1: Typical Placement Order — Connector → Protection → Filtering / Common-Mode Processing → Interface Transceiver → Controller From the board edge toward the center, a common arrangement is: Outer edge: Board-edge connector; Protection layer: TVS diodes, ceramic discharge devices, gas discharge tubes, and other ESD protection components; Filtering / common-mode layer: Common-mode chokes, ferrite beads, and filtering capacitors; Driver layer: MAX485, PHY, CAN transceivers, and other interface ICs; Core circuitry: MCU/FPGA and other main processing devices. This is a general placement approach rather than a universal rule. The actual order should be determined based on the interface standard, device datasheet, ESD current path, and EMC requirements. Ethernet, USB, CAN, RS485, and HDMI do not necessarily use the same protection and filtering structures, so the component sequence should be adapted to the specific interface PCB design. Guideline 2: Plan the Ground Plane and Return Path in the Interface Area External interfaces such as RS485, CAN, and Ethernet may require a dedicated interface ground that is isolated from the digital or analog ground on the main board. The ground structure and return path should be planned according to the isolation architecture. Avoid routing high-speed signals across reference-plane splits, which can interrupt the return path and increase radiated noise; For isolated RS485/CAN interfaces, plan the interface-side and system-side grounds according to the isolation components and isolated power architecture; When the two ground domains must be connected, select an appropriate connection method based on the isolation and EMC design, while controlling the connection location and return path to avoid unnecessary ground loops; Avoid routing signals across split regions for long distances. A good PCB layout should always consider the signal path and its corresponding return path together. Guideline 3: Treat Differential Interfaces According to Their Speed High-speed differential interfaces (USB, HDMI, LVDS, PCIe, etc.): Perform length matching according to the interface specification and device requirements, while maintaining consistent coupling within each differential pair. Key considerations include differential impedance, intra-pair skew, and reference-plane continuity. Length matching should follow the requirements of the specific interface rather than a universal numerical limit. Routing near the connector should be as straight as practical, avoiding unnecessary 90° corners and repeated bends. RS485, CAN, and similar interfaces: These interfaces generally do not require extremely strict length matching. Greater attention should be paid to topology, such as bus or star configurations, termination, return paths, and the parasitic effects of protection devices. Avoid routing unrelated signals between differential pairs to reduce crosstalk and preserve differential performance. Guideline 4: Minimize Vias in High-Speed Paths and Provide Nearby Ground Vias Keep high-speed signals on a single routing layer from the driver to the connector whenever practical, avoiding unnecessary layer transitions; If a layer transition is unavoidable, place nearby ground vias around the signal vias to provide a continuous, low-impedance return path for high-frequency currents. The exact number and spacing of ground vias should be determined based on the stackup, via dimensions, and interface speed to reduce signal distortion and radiation caused by layer transitions. 4. Conclusion Placing interface drivers close to board-edge connectors is a practical design guideline based on signal integrity (SI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), rather than an absolute rule that applies to every interface. In general, placing the driver close to the connector provides three main benefits: Shortens boundary traces and reduces high-frequency loop area, helping lower EMI radiation and interference coupling; Shortens high-speed signal paths, reduces parasitic effects, and makes controlled-impedance routing easier; Provides a low-impedance path for ESD discharge and reduces the risk of ESD-related interference to the main controller. Verify Now Blog > Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 21,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity PCB antipad high-speed PCB design anti pad pcb In high-speed PCB design , via antipads are often treated as simple clearance features. In fact, the size of a PCB antipad directly affects the parasitic capacitance and local impedance around a via, making it an important parameter for maintaining impedance continuity and signal integrity. If the antipad is too small, it can introduce excessive capacitive loading and cause local impedance to drop. If it is too large, it may affect the integrity of the power or ground plane. Especially in Gbps-level high-speed links, simply using the default parameters in PCB design software can result in significant impedance discontinuities around the via transition, potentially affecting signal integrity. The purpose of an anti pad PCB design is not limited to preventing electrical shorts. By changing the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, a properly designed antipad can reduce via parasitic capacitance, optimize local impedance, and minimize signal reflections. Therefore, antipad design is an important part of optimizing high-speed vias. What Is a PCB Antipad Actually “Removing”? Let's put aside the abstract definition and look at it from a straightforward engineering perspective. When a PCB via changes layers, its metal barrel and pad pass through portions of the power and ground planes. The metal conductor, dielectric material, and surrounding plane copper naturally form parasitic capacitance. The impedance of a transmission line is mainly determined by the dielectric material, trace width, and stackup. However, the additional parasitic capacitance around a via introduces extra capacitive loading, causing the local via impedance to deviate from the target impedance of the transmission line. This creates an impedance discontinuity that can affect high-speed signal transmission. A PCB antipad is a copper clearance area created around the via pad on the power or ground plane layers through which the via passes. Its main purposes are: Increase the distance between the via barrel and plane copper to prevent electrical shorts; Reduce the parasitic capacitance between the via and reference plane, optimize local via impedance, and reduce reflections caused by impedance discontinuity. A high-speed signal trace can be compared to a smooth road with a constant speed limit. The via is an unavoidable intersection, while parasitic capacitance is like a sudden dip in the road. When the signal travels through this discontinuity at high speed, impedance changes can cause reflections, ringing, and waveform distortion. The purpose of an antipad is to adjust the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, reducing the impact of this “dip” and making the via transition smoother. （Anti-pad Structure） How Does Parasitic Capacitance Affect Via Impedance? A via is not an ideal conductor. Its equivalent model can include parasitic inductance L and parasitic capacitance C. For high-speed signals, the actual impedance characteristics of a via are also affected by factors such as via length, hole diameter, pad size, antipad size, reference plane position, and via stub. The antipad size is one of the important parameters affecting via parasitic capacitance. If the antipad is too small, the distance between the via barrel or pad and the reference plane becomes smaller, increasing the capacitive loading between the via and plane. This can cause a more significant drop in local via impedance. For example, when a transmission line with a target impedance of 50 Ω passes through an unoptimized via structure, the local impedance may decrease around the via transition, creating a structure such as: 50 Ω trace → lower impedance at via → 50 Ω trace. This impedance discontinuity can cause signal reflections, energy loss, and waveform distortion. Therefore, an antipad is not simply a matter of making the clearance as large or as small as possible. In high-speed PCB design, its size needs to be optimized together with the stackup, via structure, and target impedance. （Small antipad vs Large antipad） What Problems Can Improper Antipad Design Cause? It is easy to assume that a small dimensional difference will not matter. However, in Gbps-level high-speed links, even small geometric changes in the via structure can affect impedance and signal integrity. 1. Impedance Discontinuity, Signal Reflection, and Reduced Eye Opening A smaller antipad → higher parasitic capacitance → potentially lower local via impedance. When a high-speed signal reaches this region, a significant impedance change can cause signal reflection, edge distortion, increased jitter, and reduced eye opening. These effects may ultimately degrade the performance of the high-speed link. 2. Poorer Return Loss and Reflected Signal Energy Impedance discontinuities increase signal reflection, causing part of the signal energy to return toward the transmitter instead of reaching the receiver effectively. For high-speed SerDes links, reflections from multiple vias, connectors, and package structures can accumulate. Therefore, maintaining impedance continuity across the via transition is an important part of signal integrity optimization. 3. Via Resonance and Stub Effects Can Increase Loss at Specific Frequencies The parasitic inductance and capacitance of a via, together with unused via stubs, can create frequency-dependent resonance and reflection characteristics. When the effective frequency range of a high-speed signal approaches these resonant regions, return loss and insertion loss may deteriorate significantly. This is one reason why some links may work normally at lower speeds but show degraded performance at higher data rates. Therefore, in addition to PCB antipad design, high-speed via design also needs to consider via stubs. For loss-sensitive high-speed links, techniques such as back drilling, blind vias, or buried vias can be used to shorten or eliminate unnecessary via stubs. 4. Reference Plane Discontinuity and Poorer Return Current Paths An antipad should not simply be made as large as possible. If the plane clearance becomes excessively large, it may affect the continuity of the local reference plane and force the high-speed return current to take a longer path. This can increase return-path inductance and introduce additional impedance discontinuities. In high-density high-speed PCB design, the locations of adjacent vias, return vias, and reference planes should also be considered together to avoid creating new signal integrity or EMI problems through excessive plane clearance. Not Just Vias: BGA Areas Also Need Attention Most high-speed PCB designs focus heavily on via antipads, but in high-density BGA regions, the parasitic capacitance between component pads and reference planes also deserves attention. A typical high-speed trace may be only 3–4 mil wide, while a BGA pad is usually much larger than the trace. The larger the pad area and the closer it is to the reference plane, the greater the potential capacitive loading. A large pad located close to a reference plane can introduce additional capacitive loading, making the BGA breakout region another potential impedance transition in a high-speed signal path. Therefore, high-speed BGA design should consider: BGA pad size; Distance between the pad and reference plane; Trace width and impedance; Breakout method; Reference plane continuity. When necessary, local plane clearance can be used to reduce the parasitic capacitance associated with the pad. However, not every BGA pad requires an enlarged antipad. Excessive plane clearance can also disrupt reference plane continuity and force the return current to detour. Therefore, the appropriate clearance should be determined based on the stackup, pad geometry, target impedance, and simulation results. How Should a Differential Via Antipad Be Designed? A single-ended signal via can typically use a circular antipad, but differential vias should not simply follow the same design approach. 1. Separate Circular Antipads May Introduce Additional Coupling If the positive and negative differential vias each use an independent circular antipad, a narrow strip of reference plane copper may remain between the two antipads. This remaining copper can change the electromagnetic coupling between the two vias. For high-speed differential signals, such a structural change may affect: Differential impedance Symmetry between the two signal paths Differential-to-common-mode conversion Insertion loss and return loss around the via transition 2. Connected Oval or “Dog-Bone” Antipad When space allows and simulation confirms the design, the antipads around the two differential vias can be partially connected to form an oval or “dog-bone” clearance area. This approach can reduce unnecessary plane copper between the two vias and create a more symmetrical electromagnetic environment around the differential via pair. The main benefits include: Better control of differential impedance toward the target value; Improved structural symmetry and reduced risk of differential-to-common-mode conversion; Reduced unnecessary local electromagnetic coupling between the vias. However, a dog-bone-shaped antipad is not a universal solution for every differential via structure. The final shape and dimensions should still be determined based on via spacing, stackup, target impedance, and simulation results. How Large Should a PCB Antipad Be? Antipad design is a typical case of “too much of a good thing.” If the antipad is too small, electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane increases, potentially increasing parasitic capacitance. If it is too large, reference plane continuity may be affected. Therefore, the PCB antipad needs to balance impedance control, return current paths, and manufacturing capability. Key Guidelines for High-Speed PCB Antipad Design 1. Do Not Simply Apply a Fixed Mil Value There is no universal antipad size that works for every high-speed PCB. The actual dimensions should be optimized according to via hole diameter, pad size, dielectric thickness, material Dk, reference plane position, and target impedance. 2. Meet Manufacturing Rules Before Optimizing Impedance An initial antipad size can be established according to the PCB manufacturer's design rules and then refined through impedance calculation or simulation. 3. Maintain Symmetry in Differential Vias For differential via structures, the geometry and electromagnetic environment around the positive and negative vias should be as symmetrical as possible to maintain differential impedance and reduce mode conversion. 4. Simulate the Complete Via Transition for High-Speed Links For high-speed links above 10 Gbps, as well as interfaces such as PCIe, USB, and SerDes that have strict requirements for channel loss and impedance continuity, fixed empirical dimensions should not be applied directly. The complete stackup, material Dk/Df, via geometry, reference planes, return vias, and target impedance should be considered together. For complex three-dimensional via structures, tools such as HFSS, CST, or Simbeor can be used for electromagnetic analysis, while tools such as Polar SI9000 are more suitable for PCB stackup and transmission-line impedance analysis. The acceptable impedance variation should ultimately be determined according to the specific interface specification and channel budget rather than applying a single universal ±10% requirement. Conclusion Effective high-speed PCB design is not simply about creating an antipad around a via. It requires an understanding of the relationship between parasitic capacitance, via impedance, reference planes, return current paths, and signal integrity. An antipad that is too small may increase capacitive loading and cause local impedance to decrease, while an oversized antipad may affect reference plane continuity. For high-speed differential vias, designers must also consider structural symmetry, differential impedance, and mode conversion. Therefore, there is no single antipad size that is suitable for every PCB. A properly designed PCB antipad should be optimized according to the target impedance and signal integrity requirements, together with the PCB stackup, via geometry, manufacturing capability, and simulation results. This helps maintain a more continuous and stable electromagnetic environment throughout the high-speed signal path. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS Why ICs Fail After Passing ESD Tests and How ESD Differs from EOS by: Mila Sep 14,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout ESD protection esd protection circuit Previous articles have covered key technologies related to chip ESD, including ESD diodes, power clamps, CDM mechanisms, and ESD testing procedures, with a focus on chip-level electrostatic discharge protection. However, a common problem in real-world engineering applications is that an IC may pass all standard ESD tests but still suffer damage or failure when used on an actual customer circuit board. Engineers often assume that the problem is insufficient chip-level ESD protection. However, this judgment has limitations. Not all electrical failures are caused by ESD. In many real-world applications, the underlying cause may instead be EOS (Electrical Overstress). 1. What Is EOS? EOS stands for Electrical Overstress. It refers to a condition in which an IC is subjected to voltage, current, or power stress beyond its designed safe operating limits, resulting in electrical abnormalities or physical damage. Common EOS Scenarios EOS can occur in many real-world application conditions, including: Power supply overvoltage I/O input voltage exceeding the specified limit Output short circuits Hot-plugging transients Line surge events Power supply reversal Negative voltage stress Ground bounce Abnormal power sequencing EOS is not a single standardized failure test model. Instead, it is a general term for failures caused by excessive electrical stress. Any voltage, current, or power stress that exceeds the device's designed tolerance can potentially result in EOS failure. 2. Key Differences Between EOS and ESD Both ESD and EOS can cause electrical damage to an IC, which is why they are easily confused in engineering practice. However, they differ significantly in terms of stress characteristics, duration, energy, and failure mechanisms. （Comparison of ESD and EOS Waveforms） 3. Why Can an IC Fail After Passing ESD Tests? Passing standardized HBM and CDM tests only demonstrates that an IC can withstand specific short-duration electrostatic discharge stresses under defined test conditions. It does not mean that the device can withstand every type of electrical transient that may occur in a real system. Standard ESD Tests Have Limited Coverage Standard ESD tests are designed around defined test models and conditions. They verify whether an IC's ESD protection structures and discharge paths can safely handle specified electrostatic pulses. However, these tests cannot reproduce every electrical stress that may occur after the IC is integrated into a complete circuit board. Real-World Applications Introduce Different Electrical Stress In actual circuit board applications, electrical stress may come from: Cable insertion and removal Power-on overshoot External load short circuits Surge coupling through long cables Back-EMF from motors, relays, and other inductive loads Transient ground potential rise Abnormal sequencing between multiple power domains Accidental power connection Compared with standardized ESD pulses, these events may have longer durations, higher accumulated energy, or repeated stress characteristics, resulting in different types of IC damage. The internal ESD protection circuit of an IC is primarily designed to handle short-duration electrostatic pulses. Its purpose is to establish a controlled discharge path and divert transient energy. Therefore, passing ESD tests does not mean that an IC has system-level protection against all EOS conditions. （ESD Test PASS vs Real PCB FAIL） 4. The Functional Limits of Internal ESD Protection A common misconception in system design is that an IC can withstand all external electrical disturbances simply because its pins include an ESD protection circuit. In practice, this assumption can create significant reliability risks. What Is Internal ESD Protection Designed For? The internal ESD protection structure is an important protection layer against electrostatic events. It is designed to provide a low-impedance path for short-duration ESD currents and prevent excessive voltage from reaching sensitive internal circuits. However, this protection is not intended to absorb large amounts of energy for an extended period. It should therefore not be treated as a substitute for system-level EOS protection. What Happens Under Sustained Overvoltage? For example, if an I/O pin is continuously exposed to a voltage beyond its specified operating range and the internal protection structure enters conduction, current may continue to flow into or through the IC. As the stress continues, the protection device and related circuits can generate significant heat. Depending on the electrical stress and internal current path, this may eventually cause damage to components such as: I/O protection devices Output driver circuits Power clamp structures Metal interconnects Vias PN junctions Core input circuits The actual damage location depends on the magnitude and duration of the external stress as well as the current path inside the IC. Common board-level protection methods include: TVS devices Series current-limiting resistors Power clamps Fuses Overcurrent protection Appropriate grounding Proper PCB layout The goal is not simply to add more protection components, but to limit the voltage, current, and energy that can reach the IC and provide a controlled path for transient energy. （Board-Level Protection + IC Internal ESD Protection） 5. Typical EOS Damage Locations and Failure Analysis EOS damage is closely related to the actual current path created by the electrical stress. Different types of stress can affect different areas of the IC: Power supply overvoltage: May damage power clamp structures, internal power circuits, metal interconnects, and thin gate-oxide devices. I/O input overvoltage: May damage I/O protection structures, input circuits, pull-up or pull-down protection structures, and core gate circuits. Output short circuit: May damage output driver circuits, metal interconnects, vias, and local diffusion regions. Negative voltage stress: May damage I/O protection structures, junction regions, and input/output circuits. Therefore, EOS failure analysis should not rely solely on the appearance of a localized burn mark. It is more important to trace the source of the electrical stress, current entry and exit paths, stress duration, and energy to identify the root cause. 6. Engineering Differences Between ESD and EOS Failure Signatures There is no absolute method for distinguishing ESD from EOS based solely on physical failure signatures. However, practical failure analysis often reveals some characteristic differences that can be used as initial clues. Common ESD failure characteristics include: Localized single-point damage Gate-oxide breakdown Abnormalities around I/O protection structures Localized PN-junction leakage Leakage or parameter changes at a single pin Common EOS failure characteristics include: More obvious thermal damage Localized melting or burning of metal Significant thermal damage to vias or metal interconnects Large-area circuit damage Abnormalities along power paths Damage to output driver circuits Simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins or circuit nodes It is important to note that these failure signatures are only supporting evidence and should not be treated as final conclusions. Accurate differentiation between ESD and EOS failures requires comprehensive analysis of the failure scenario, electrical test data, application environment, test conditions, damage location, and physical analysis results. 7. The Risks of Misdiagnosing EOS as ESD In real-world applications, misdiagnosing an EOS failure as insufficient ESD protection can lead to an incorrect corrective strategy, wasting design resources while leaving the actual problem unresolved. When an IC is damaged by system-level EOS, simply increasing the size of the internal ESD protection structure, strengthening the internal power clamp, or widening internal metal interconnects generally cannot solve the system-level failure. The root cause may instead be related to board-level electrical stress, such as excessive external surge energy, improper TVS selection, continuous power supply overvoltage, load short circuits, abnormal hot-plug timing, or the lack of an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path for inductive loads. The key risk of misdiagnosing EOS is that engineers may continue to optimize the chip's ESD protection circuit without addressing the actual source and energy path of the system-level electrical stress. As a result, the same failure may occur repeatedly. Therefore, when investigating electrical failures in real-world applications, both chip-level and system-level factors should be considered rather than focusing only on the internal ESD structure. 8. Key Questions for Troubleshooting Suspected EOS Failures When an IC experiences an electrical failure, the following factors can be checked first to avoid automatically classifying the problem as an ESD failure: Failure Scenario Did the failure occur during a standard ESD test or during actual customer operation? Did it occur at the moment of power-up, during cable insertion or removal, after a load short circuit, or when a motor or relay was activated? Failure Location Is the problem limited to leakage at a single I/O pin, a low-resistance path between the power supply and ground, or simultaneous abnormalities across multiple pins? Has the overall operating current of the IC changed significantly? Stress Characteristics Was the failure caused by a short-duration transient pulse, continuous overvoltage, or overcurrent? Was there any periodic or repeated electrical stress or abnormal power sequencing? Board-Level Protection Does the circuit board include TVS or other surge protection? Is an appropriate current-limiting circuit provided? Does the power supply have overvoltage or clamping protection? Does the grounding path provide sufficiently low impedance? Does the inductive load have an appropriate freewheeling or clamping path? These factors can help determine whether the failure is related to system-level EOS and provide a basis for tracing the electrical stress path into the IC. Conclusion Both ESD and EOS can cause IC leakage, short circuits, functional abnormalities, and physical damage, but their stress characteristics, protection strategies, and corrective measures are significantly different. Passing standard ESD tests only verifies the IC's ability to withstand specific short-duration electrostatic pulses and does not cover every overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, power reversal, or ground-bounce condition that may occur in a real system. Therefore, when investigating an IC failure in an actual application, engineers should not determine the root cause solely based on the fact that the device passed ESD testing or on the appearance of localized physical damage. Instead, the failure scenario, electrical stress, failure location, current path, board-level protection, and physical analysis results should be considered together. For electrical stress outside standard ESD test conditions, such as overvoltage, overcurrent, surge, hot-plugging, and inductive load transients, EOS should be considered as a potential root cause. Appropriate board-level protection can help limit the voltage, current, and energy reaching the IC and reduce the risk of application-level failure. Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. Very rewarding and highly recommended Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport.
